content: The Germanic languages form a distinct branch of the Indo-European language family. They share a common ancestor, Proto-Germanic, which was spoken in northern Europe during the Iron Age, around the mid-1st millennium BC. Proto-Germanic and its descendant languages are defined by unique linguistic features, including the consonant shift known as Grimm's Law. The Germanic languages first entered recorded history with the Germanic peoples who settled along the borders of the Roman Empire in northern Europe during the 2nd century AD. Among the Germanic languages, English and German are the most widely spoken, with approximately 400 million and 100 million native speakers, respectively. Other significant languages in this group include Dutch, with 23 million speakers, and Afrikaans, with over 16 million speakers. The North Germanic languages, such as Norwegian, Danish, Swedish, Icelandic, and Faroese, collectively have about 20 million speakers. According to the SIL Ethnologue, there are 53 distinct Germanic languages. Linguistic Characteristics Germanic languages exhibit several unique features: The simplification of the Indo-European tense and aspect system into a present tense and a past tense (preterite). A large class of verbs, known as weak verbs, that form their past tense using a dental suffix (/d/ or /t/) rather than vowel alternation (ablaut). Verbs that retain vowel alternation are called strong verbs. The use of strong and weak adjectives, with different inflectional endings depending on the definiteness of the noun phrase. Modern English adjectives no longer inflect, except for comparative and superlative forms, but Old English followed this system. The consonant shift known as Grimm's Law, which affected the sounds of consonants in Germanic languages. High German underwent an additional consonant shift, known as the High German consonant shift. A set of words with etymologies that are difficult to trace to other Indo-European families but are found across nearly all Germanic languages, supporting the Germanic substrate hypothesis. A shift in stress accent to the root of the stem and later to the first syllable of the word. While English has irregular stress patterns, native words consistently maintain fixed stress regardless of affixes. Germanic languages differ significantly from one another, more so than some other language families like Romance or Slavic. These differences reflect varying degrees of conservatism or progressiveness in their evolution toward analytic structures. For example, languages like German, Dutch, and Icelandic have preserved much of the complex inflectional morphology inherited from Proto-Indo-European, while English, Swedish, and Afrikaans have become more analytic. Another notable feature of Germanic languages is the verb-second (V2) word order, which is rare cross-linguistically. This structure is present in all modern Germanic languages except modern English, which historically had V2 but has largely replaced it with a subject-verb-object (SVO) syntax. Writing Systems The earliest evidence of Germanic languages comes from names recorded by Tacitus in the 1st century AD, particularly in his work Germania. The first instance of Germanic writing appears on the Negau helmet from the 2nd century BC. By the 2nd century AD, early Germanic speakers developed the Elder Futhark, an early form of the Runic alphabet. Early Runic inscriptions primarily consist of personal names and are challenging to interpret. The Gothic language was written using the Gothic alphabet, created by Bishop Ulfilas in the 4th century for his Bible translation. Later, Christian priests and monks, fluent in Latin and their native Germanic varieties, began writing Germanic languages using slightly modified Latin letters. However, during the Viking Age, Runic alphabets remained in common use in Scandinavia. Many Germanic languages today use the standard Latin alphabet, often supplemented with accent marks and additional letters such as umlauts (ä, ö, ü), ß (Eszett), and others like Ø, Æ, Å, Þ, and Ð. Historical Development All Germanic languages are believed to descend from Proto-Germanic, which underwent sound shifts described by Grimm's Law and Verner's Law. These changes likely occurred during the Pre-Roman Iron Age in northern Europe, around 500 BC. Other shared innovations suggest a common history of pre-Proto-Germanic speakers during the Nordic Bronze Age. From their earliest attestations, Germanic varieties are divided into three groups: West, East, and North Germanic. Their exact relationships are difficult to determine due to limited evidence from Runic inscriptions. These varieties remained mutually intelligible during the Migration Period, making classification challenging. For example, the 6th-century Lombardic language may have originated as a North or East Germanic variety but became assimilated into West Germanic as the Lombards settled near the Elbe River. The West Germanic group likely formed during the late Jastorf culture, while the East Germanic group may have originated from 1st-century varieties in Gotland. Southern Sweden is considered the original location of the North Germanic group. The earliest coherent Germanic text is the 4th-century Gothic translation of the New Testament by Ulfilas. Early West Germanic evidence includes scattered Old High German words and sentences from the 6th century and coherent texts from the 9th century. Old English texts appear by the 10th century. North Germanic is attested in scattered Runic inscriptions as Proto-Norse until it evolved into Old Norse around 800 AD. Longer Runic inscriptions survive from the 8th and 9th centuries, while longer Latin-alphabet texts appear from the 12th century. By the 10th century, Germanic varieties had diverged enough to hinder mutual intelligibility. The Viking settlers in the Danelaw influenced the English language, likely contributing to the collapse of Old English grammar and the emergence of Middle English in the 12th century. East Germanic languages were marginalized after the Migration Period, with groups like the Burgundians, Goths, and Vandals becoming linguistically assimilated by the 7th century. Crimean Gothic persisted until the 18th century. During the early Middle Ages, West Germanic languages diverged further due to the insular development of Middle English and the High German consonant shift on the continent. This resulted in Upper German, Low Saxon, and intermediate Central German varieties. By the Early Modern period, these differences had expanded significantly, with extremes like Highest Alemannic in the south and Northern Low Saxon in the north being barely mutually intelligible. Southern varieties completed the second sound shift, while northern varieties remained unaffected. North Germanic languages, in contrast, remained more unified, with the peninsular languages retaining mutual intelligibility into modern times. Classification The divisions among Germanic subfamilies are rarely precise, as most form continuous dialect continua. Adjacent varieties are often mutually intelligible, while more distant ones are not.
